newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia considers rights watch over Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Australia considers rights watch over Hong Kong.

text.p: Australia said on Tuesday it would consider producing annual human rights reports on Hong Kong and pressing Beijing to establish a rights commission after China regains control of the British territory from July 1.
An Australian parliamentary committee on Monday criticised China's human rights record and urged Canberra to encourage the protection of democracy and rights in the territory.
"China's record on human rights needs to be faced as an impediment to confidence in Hong Kong," the committee said in a report on Hong Kong's future under Chinese rule.
A spokesman for Foreign Minister Alexander Downer told Rueters the Foreign Affairs Department would consider the report and make its own recommendations to Downer.
Australia and China have already agreed to establish an unprecedented bilateral human rights dialogue, which would also cover Hong Kong.

The parliamentary committee criticised Britain for failing to create a democratic culture in Hong Kong, saying London's failure left the territory's human rights and democratic institutions vulnerable.

It called on Canberra to make annual reports on political and human rights for the first five years of Chinese rule, press Beijing to set up a human rights commission in the territory, and offer assistance, including the service of Australian judges to help the independence of the territory's courts.

Australia's conservative Liberal-National government has adopted a low-key to human rights in China after a series of spats over diplomatic and security issues soured relations between the two trading partners.

Announcing the planned human rights dialogue -- set to begin in August -- Downer said in April that Canberra had abandoned its traditional support for a United Nations motion censuring China for rights abuses. That motion, at the U.N. Human Rights Commission, was defeated for the seventh time since 1990.
Communist China resumes control of the free market territory on July 1, ending 156 years of British rule.
Beijing has promised the territory considerable autonomy and survival of its social and economic system and basic freedoms.
Hong Kong's democracy movement on Monday said it would stage a protest March on July 1 to test China's pledge that free expression would survive the handover.
